Embedded mechanics has always appealed to me because it sits at the point where careful investigation meets practical impact: when small mechanical changes can be translated into devices that improve quality, safety, and real-world outcomes. That is why I am pursuing a Biomedical Engineer role, where I can blend curiosity, problem-solving, and a genuine interest in how machines work into work that can improve patient outcomes. I am originally from Bangladesh, and I hold a Bachelor’s degree from a university not listed in the major global rankings. Through that academic foundation, I developed a strong interest in turning technical knowledge into dependable results, and I completed 2 projects with tangible outcomes that strengthened my understanding of how careful testing and analysis can support real-world medical applications.

My background has also shaped how I approach technical work. In one role, I needed to use a new tool and became comfortable with it within a few weeks, which allowed me to contribute productively to the team’s workflow. On another project, I noticed that a recurring bottleneck was slowing progress, so I introduced a simple adjustment to the process that reduced repeated delays and saved the team time. Teammates have also occasionally asked me to look over work in my own area before submission, which reflects the importance of careful checking and shared standards. During a long assignment that included setbacks and revisions, I kept the work moving over an extended period and put in extra time when needed to bring it through to completion.

What keeps this career personal for me is how visible its impact can be. One of my favourite memories is bringing my family to an open house at a manufacturing facility where I worked and watching them light up as I explained how the machines on the floor were built and optimised; a relative joked that I “can’t look at a conveyor belt without trying to redesign it,” and that line still appears in family stories. I am now eager to bring that same practical curiosity, steady learning, and commitment to a Biomedical Engineer position where I can contribute to reliable, efficient, and meaningful medical progress.

Nothing is more rewarding to me than the moment a child suddenly understands a new idea and begins to believe they can do more than they first thought. That is why I chose primary education: to help shape a positive, curious foundation for lifelong learning and to make the classroom a place where every child feels seen, encouraged, and capable. Originally from Colombia, I bring this perspective alongside a Master’s degree from a university ranked in the global top 100, and through that academic path I completed 4 projects with tangible outcomes, each reinforcing my interest in turning ideas into practical results. One of my favourite memories is of a younger family member proudly demonstrating the classic “bridge game” method I had taught them to relatives at a school reading event, turning it into an impromptu reading-game challenge that brought home for me how engaging and inclusive the classroom can be.

My professional development has been shaped by steady, practical experience. In one role, I needed to use a new technique that the work required; within a couple of months I had learned it well enough to apply it independently in my own tasks. On another occasion, I noticed that the team was repeatedly losing time at the same stage of a process, so I introduced a simple adjustment that reduced delays and saved time across the group. Colleagues now and then come to me with questions in areas they know I have worked on, and I value those moments because they reflect the importance of sharing knowledge in a collaborative environment. I also took the initiative to begin a substantial piece of work beyond my formal role and carried it through over many months until it was completed.

What continues to draw me to primary teaching is the chance to create engaging, inclusive lessons that adapt to different learning styles while keeping the classroom calm, positive, and purposeful. I am now eager to bring my background, care for children’s progress, and commitment to purposeful, inclusive learning into a Primary School Teacher role, where I can continue helping children grow in confidence, curiosity, and understanding.
